title: The rainbow (Genesis 9:8–17)
hook: God's first covenant is with all living things, and the bow in the cloud is its sign

segments.voice: Yesterday: yonah, the dove with a freshly plucked leaf, the first sign the flood was easing. Your line was the leaf comes back.

The door of the ark opens. Out come Noah, his wife, his sons and their wives, then the animals, blinking, into a washed-out world. The ground is mud. Everything they knew is gone. And the first thing God does is make a promise. Not only to Noah. The Torah is almost fussy about the guest list: to you, and to your children after you, and to every living creature that is with you, the fowl, the cattle, every beast of the earth. Never again, God says, will a flood destroy the earth. Then God points at the sky after the rain, at something every child has stopped to stare at.
screen: `THE DOOR OPENS ONTO MUD.` → `A PROMISE WITH A GUEST LIST.` → `EVERY LIVING CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Brit. A covenant: a binding promise between two sides. The word runs all through Jewish life. A baby boy's circumcision is a brit milah, the covenant of circumcision. Sinai will be a brit. But here's what's striking. This covenant, the first one the Torah spells out, isn't with Abraham, and it isn't with Israel. It's with everyone: every person, every animal, the whole earth. In the old JPS translation: "I have set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between Me and the earth." The bow is keshet, the ordinary Hebrew word for a rainbow, and also for a bow, the weapon. Some commentators noticed that a rainbow looks like a bow with its ends pointing down toward the ground, aimed away from the earth: a weapon hung up in the sky. The rabbis built something lasting on this covenant. They taught that all people, the children of Noah, are bound by seven basic laws, among them not to murder, not to steal, and to set up courts of justice. An early rabbinic teaching says the righteous of every nation have a share in the world to come. And there's a blessing, from the Talmud, for seeing a rainbow: it praises God who remembers the covenant and keeps the promise. In the story, a rainbow is a promise God made to every living thing, and people stop in parking lots to look at it.
screen: `BRIT — A BINDING PROMISE.` · `THE FIRST COVENANT IS WITH ALL.` · `KESHET — A BOW HUNG UP.` · `THE SEVEN LAWS OF NOAH.` · then, large: `A TOKEN OF A COVENANT.`

segments.voice: Think of one promise small enough to actually keep: I'll call my mother on Sunday, I'll put my phone away at dinner, I'll feed the birds this week. Say it to yourself quietly, and picture keeping it. If you pray, you can offer it in your prayer; if not, just let it settle, because a covenant starts with one promise kept.
Brit. A covenant, and the first one is with every living thing. That ends the fifth week: clothes for the road, Cain and Abel, my brother's keeper, tzaddik, the ark, the dove, and brit.
Your line: a promise to everything. Even the cattle made the guest list. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: A short blessing from the Talmud is said on seeing a rainbow, praising God who remembers the covenant; the idea of the seven Noahide laws for all humanity comes from this covenant with Noah.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: "one of the biggest words" softened; "the first brit" now "the first one the Torah spells out" (6:18 already mentions a covenant with Noah); the Noahide line now quotes the actual early teaching (Tosefta: the righteous of the nations have a share in the world to come) instead of an unconditional "anyone is righteous"; "many Jews say" cut; the rainbow-as-promise line framed as the story, not narrator fact.
